### Oxygen Partial Pressure Calculation

At an oxygen concentration of 30% ($0.30$) and a total atmospheric pressure of 10.2 psi, the oxygen partial pressure ($P_{\text{O}_2}$) is calculated as follows:

$$P_{\text{O}_2} = 0.30 \times 10.2 \text{ psi} = 3.06 \text{ psi} \quad [\text{C-001}]$$

This pressure regime represents the anticipated intermediate atmosphere for lunar operations ( l.e., $\text{O}_2 \ge 30\%$ at a total pressure $P \le 10.2 \text{ psi}$) [F-005].

---

### Comparison with Earth Sea-Level Air

1. **Earth Sea-Level Oxygen Partial Pressure**:
   At Earth's sea level, total atmospheric pressure is 14.7 psi [F-002]. Assuming standard air with an $\text{O}_2$ fraction of 20.9% ($0.209$), the oxygen partial pressure is:
   $$P_{\text{O}_2, \text{sea level}} = 0.209 \times 14.7 \text{ psi} = 3.072 \text{ psi} \quad [\text{C-002}]$$

2. **Ratio of Partial Pressures**:
   Comparing the 10.2 psi / 30% $\text{O}_2$ atmosphere to Earth sea-level air yields:
   $$\frac{3.06 \text{ psi}}{3.072 \text{ psi}} \approx 0.996 \text{ (or } 99.6\% \text{ of sea-level } P_{\text{O}_2}\text{)}$$
   Thus, the absolute oxygen partial pressure at 30% $\text{O}_2$ and 10.2 psi (3.06 psi) [C-001] is virtually equivalent to Earth sea-level air (3.072 psi) [C-002].

3. **Oxygen Concentration Difference**:
   While $P_{\text{O}_2}$ remains equivalent, the oxygen mole fraction increases from 20.9% to 30.0%, representing a relative concentration increase of approximately 43.5% over ambient air [C-004].

---

### Flammability Assessment Considerations

When assessing material flammability and spacecraft fire safety under these conditions, fire risk must not be evaluated based on oxygen percentage or partial pressure alone. Total atmospheric pressure, inert diluent gas composition (e.g., $\text{N}_2$), and ambient ventilation flow velocity must all be evaluated simultaneously to accurately characterize flammability risks.

bundle.question: What is the oxygen partial pressure at 30% O2 and 10.2 psi, and how does it compare with sea-level air?

facts.claim: Spacesuits are pressurized with 100% oxygen up to only 4.3 psi.
At sea level on Earth, atmospheric pressure is 14.7 psi.
To prevent decompression sickness ('the bends'), astronauts perform a pre-breathe protocol by inhaling 100% oxygen to purge dissolved nitrogen from body tissues.

To reduce pre-breathe times and facilitate lunar surface extravehicular activities (EVAs), the atmosphere in lunar habitats and pressurized rovers is anticipated to have pressure and oxygen concentration intermediate between spacesuits and Earth sea-level atmosphere.
The intermediate atmosphere for lunar operations is anticipated to feature an oxygen concentration of 30% or higher, with a total pressure of 10.2 psi or lower.

The suppressants are carbon dioxide and helium. The expected concentrations range from 0.00 mole
fraction to the limit where no flame can exist (0.70 expected for the least active suppressant). Pressure: Ambient pressure does not significantly influence the droplet burning rate, but does influence
chemistry at sufficiently low values. In addition, one strategy for extinguishing a fire is to isolate the
habitat where it exists and vent the cabin to space. It is therefore beneficial to have verified suppressant
data at low pressures. The pressure for the tests will range from 0.5 to 1.0 atm (standard atmosphere). As
with the oxygen mole fraction, it is important that the test chamber be sufficiently large so that the
pressure is essentially constant during an experiment (i.e. the droplet burns in a constant pressure
ambient). Fuel Type: The advantage of the droplet geometry is that the fuel is relatively simple and better
characterized than typical fuels in fire safety studies (e.g. PMMA or paper). This is also a disadvantage
since it does not represent a practical fuel. The study will use two typical hydrocarbon fuels, an alcohol,
methanol (CH3OH ) and an alkane, heptane (C7H16 ). There is a relatively large experience base with
these fuels. Methanol has a fuel-bound oxygen atom, and burns with a very dim blue flame (not much
soot production) with a small standoff distance, so it has widely different radiative characteristics than
heptane.

[BASS-II | S-011: Science Requirements Document (SRD) for BASS-II | Objectives:]
Objectives:
• To identify what is the worst case for material flammability in spacecraft
environments, and how does that compare to the terrestrial upward burning used to
screen the materials for safe use aboard spacecraft. • To determine how quickly a fire in space can grow and if the flames reach a finite size
or continue to grow. This has implications for firefighting strategies in spacecraft. Primary variables: The main variables to be tested are the effects of ambient oxygen
concentration, ventilation flow velocity, and fuel type, thickness, and geometry.

rules.rule: Do NOT extrapolate microgravity results directly to Lunar or Martian gravity without explicitly stating the lack of direct partial-gravity empirical data and explaining bounding logic ([F-019], [F-021]).

When queried regarding combustion in Lunar or Martian gravity, explicitly clarify that NASA PSI currently contains no partial-gravity test data [F-019]. Mention E-FIELD electric field chemi-ion simulation [F-020] and 0-g/1-g bounding methodology [F-021] if relevant.

Never assess spacecraft fire flammability solely on oxygen percentage. Always evaluate oxygen partial pressure (via calculation), total pressure, diluent inert species (N2, CO2, He), and ventilation forced flow velocity together.
If asked about rocket engine or thruster propellant fires, clearly state that propulsion systems are outside the scope of PSI microgravity science due to momentum-dominated flow regimes [F-022].

For every experimental finding reported, cite the exact test conditions: fuel type, geometry, oxygen concentration, ambient pressure, flow velocity, and hardware facility. If a condition is omitted in the source, label it as 'unspecified'; do NOT guess.
If an empirical value or data point is absent from the indexed chunks and Golden Table, state 'data not available in repository'. Never fabricate numerical values from LLM parametric memory.
When source documents report conflicting findings or values, present both sources with their respective document citations, PI names, and publication years; do not arbitrarily select one.

Clearly distinguish between empirical flight experiment findings (PSI / peer-reviewed reports), challenge guidelines, mathematical derivations, and speculative engineering hypotheses. Never present interpretation as an empirical fact.
